newsitem.title: USA: Russia's reformists face test of strike, IMF visit.
newsitem.headline: Russia's reformists face test of strike, IMF visit.

text.p: Russia's nationwide strike on Thursday will focus attention on whether President Boris Yeltsin's new reformist team deals with the country's social crisis without resorting to printing money, U.S. specialists on the Russia economy said.
Angry and frustrated workers are demanding pensions and wages arrears, which have soared to some 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion).
Trade union organizers in Russia estimated 20 million workers would join the nationwide protest, making it the largest demonstration in the country since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"There is a ground swell of discontent and it has definitely been tapped by the opposition," said Richard Ericson, professor of Russian economics at Columbia University.

To mollify protesters, the Russian government is likely to pay some of the arrears through short-term borrowing and shifting of tax revenues. But such "Band-Aid" measures would not address the long-term deficits in public finances, he said.

Indeed, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, on the eve of the strikes, promised Russia would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2.1 billion) in back wages and pensions in March, and that the Russian government would pay almost three trillion roubles of that. He did not specify where the money would come from.
Erison said a large portion of the arrears had been generated for poor economic reasons, such as bloated payrolls in firms which produced unmarketable goods.
"If they just pay the bills without making substantial changes," he said, "there is some chance the IMF has to pull the plug."

International Monetary Fund director Michel Camdessus is going to Moscow on April 1 to meet President Boris Yeltsin's new cabinet and to decide whether to release overdue tranches of its $10 billion loan to Russia, which have been delayed mainly due to poor tax collection.

Gretchen Rodkey, East European and Russian debt analyst at Bear, Stearns and Co Inc, agreed that with the IMF team watching its every move, the Russian government would be restrained from making unrealistic promises.
"It is a bad time to make commitments that they cannot keep," she said, referring to the debut of the new team under the two first deputy prime ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
Pitting regional leaders against the central government, Thursday's protest will focus on the sensitive issues of local autonomy, which must be clarified before drafting the new tax code, she said.
Foreign investors generally took Camdessus' visit to Moscow as a reassuring sign that the IMF would find some way for Russia to get the withheld $900 million disbursement.
"From the moment that Camdessus said he was going to Russia, you know the deal is going to happen," said Eric Fine, an analyst at Morgan Stanley.
The strikes, while grabbing news headlines, should not affect Russia's ability to pay its external debt, he noted, saying, "It is not a credit issue."
But the enthusiasm of foreign investors over Russia's debt has flagged badly since the beginning of the year.
Russian debt papers, including restructured loans on a when-issued basis, Ministry of Finance bonds and eurobonds, have underperformed other emerging markets debt.

While the broad J.P. Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index (EMBI+) rose 3.3 percent year-to-date, the Russia subindex fell 2.74 percent. Last year, Russia was the best performing sector, soaring 114.25 percent.

Russian papers sold off sharply on Wednesday in the general bearish atmosphere of rising U.S. interest rates. For the first time in two years, the U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
A big block of Russian principle RUPRIN=RR was dumped on the market, pushing prices down to 56-7/8, off 1-3/8 on the day.
"It's flight to quality," said a trader.
Against the backdrop of strikes over back wages, foreign investors naturally would wonder if the Russian government cannot pay its own workers, could it pay its foreign debt, he added.
